Known automation; demonstrates the rate rule is not enforcing (R-10 candidate), but a site-wide Block would knock out this load tool and any shared-egress client — keep in Count.

**Known automation:**
- 198.51.100.10 — Artillery load-testing tool, UA `Artillery (https://artillery.io)`, 99.6% of window, 15 fixed URIs (GET /cart, /catalog, /home; POST /cart, /checkout, /checkout/payment, /checkout/delivery), flat high rate, no threat labels, all ALLOW. Reported as fact, not a threat. Excluded from the "who is attacking" baseline.

**AI-generated: findings need human verification before anyone acts on them.**

**Findings:**
- **Symptom:** 19:09:29–19:19:02 UTC, one browser-UA client (198.51.100.40) multi-vector injection scan: 225 requests, 210 blocked, 15 allowed, targeting query arguments, body and HTTP headers.
- **Cause 1 (detected, not blocked — missed by rule):** 198.51.100.40 — `traversal-lfi` ×15 on `/catalog` reached origin (ALLOW). No managed sub-rule matched this path-traversal in the query-argument/URI-path location, although `GenericLFI_QUERYARGUMENTS` (CommonRuleSet, present at Priority 3) blocked 30 other LFI attempts from the same client. For 198.51.100.40 specifically, a path-scoped Count→Block on the matched signatures.

{"id": "16e05689-fd2e-4420-97b2-4b2d5344caba", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "ebee6444-c280-430a-9c83-407f547f6639", "content": [{"text": "     1	---
     2	name: aws-waf-log-analysis
     3	description: >-
     4	  Use this skill when an investigation is about users, partners, scripts, or mobile apps that are
     5	  denied access to or can't reach an application behind AWS WAF (HTTP 403, 405, 202 challenge
     6	  responses, a 4xx spike, or an outage on CloudFront, ALB, or API Gateway where WAF must be ruled
     7	  out), when you need to find which WAF rule, Anti-DDoS rule, or Shield Advanced automatic
     8	  mitigation blocked, challenged, or CAPTCHA'd requests and whether it is a false positive, or
     9	  when an investigation is requested to hunt for malicious, scanning, bot, or abusive traffic in
     10	  WAF logs (no alarm needed), to find out what AWS WAF did with suspicious or unusual requests, or
     11	  to check what WAF detected but did not block.
     12	  Discovers the Web ACL and its log destination, queries WAF logs with CloudWatch Logs Insights or
     13	  Amazon Athena, falls back to WAF metrics and sampled requests, records evidence-backed findings
     14	  with advisory, narrowly scoped fixes, and writes a threat-hunt report.
     15	metadata:
     16	  author: lkna
     17	  version: "1.0.0"
     18	  aws-devops-agent-skills.agent-types: "Incident RCA"
     19	  aws-devops-agent-skills.aws-services: "AWS WAF, AWS Shield, Amazon CloudFront, Elastic Load Balancing, Amazon API Gateway, Amazon CloudWatch, Amazon Athena"
     20	  aws-devops-agent-skills.technical-domains: "Security, Networking"
     21	---
     22	
     23	# AWS WAF Log Analysis
     24	
     25	Find out whether AWS WAF (including Anti-DDoS rules and Shield Advanced automatic mitigation) is denying legitimate traffic (Mode A). Or hunt WAF logs for threats, including what WAF detected but did not block (Mode B).
     26	
     27	## Purpose and guarantees
     28	
     29	- **Read-only.** Use only Describe, Get and List calls, plus `logs:StartQuery`/`GetQueryResults`, `athena:StartQueryExecution` (SELECT only, when permitted)/`GetQueryResults`, `cloudtrail:LookupEvents`, `wafv2:GetSampledRequests` and `cloudwatch:GetMetricData`.
     30	- Never run DDL. Never change a Web ACL, rule, IP set, Shield setting, log configuration or any other resource.
     31	- **Advisory.** Describe fixes in prose for a human to review and apply. Never apply them.
     32	- **Single-turn.** Never ask the user a question and never wait for input. Apply "Defaults when input is missing", record every default under "Assumptions", and continue.
     33	- **Never stop on a gap.** A denied call or a missing table moves you to the next source or the degraded path. It does not end the investigation.
     34	- **Exact errors.** Record the exact error code. Call something "not permitted" only on `AccessDenied`/`UnauthorizedOperation`.
     35	  - A cancelled, timed-out or throttled call is retried once, then reported as not completed.
     36	  - A tool refusal such as "service operations are not allowed" means: run the call in a subagent.
     37	- **Records are the deliverable.** In both modes the investigation records (symptoms, observations, findings, gaps, hypotheses) are what is judged and shown; the last message closes them (see "Output").
     38	- **Final output.** The answer is complete as delivered. It never ends with a question or an offer. Never call `ask_user` (or any ask tool), not even after the answer to offer follow-up work or a fix: a turn that ends on a tool call loses the answer. Put follow-ups in "Next steps" and end on plain text.
     39	
     40	## Pick the mode from the request
     41	
     42	Inputs are the investigation request text, plus any attached incident or alarm details (alarm name, metric, resource, start time). A threat hunt needs no alarm: a user-requested investigation with hunting language is Mode B. Classify, and record the choice under "Assumptions".
     43	
     44	| Request contains | Mode |
     45	|---|---|
     46	| Denial or error symptoms: 403/405/202, "blocked", "can't access", "unreachable", "partner integration failing", a 4xx/5xx spike, timeouts, or an alarm on a front-door resource | **Mode A**, starting with the A0 rule-out |
     47	| Hunting language: "malicious", "scan", "attack", "bots", "is WAF missing anything", "review WAF logs", a scheduled or recurring review | **Mode B** |
     48	| Both | Mode A first, then Mode B on the same window, focused on the slice Mode A found |
     49	| Neither, but the incident involves a resource that a Web ACL protects | **A0 rule-out only**; if A0 finds WAF implicated or inconclusive, continue with A1 to A7 |
     50	
     51	When Mode A's verdict is `CORRECT_MITIGATION` (a real attack), recommend Mode B on that slice. Run it in the same investigation when the request is in scope for hunting.
     52	
     53	## Defaults when input is missing
     54	
     55	Never ask. Apply the default and record it. Read "Defaults when input is missing (full table)" in [discovery-and-log-sources.md](references/discovery-and-log-sources.md) when an input below is missing and you need the exact fallback.
     56	
     57	- **Time window:** Mode A: incident start minus 30 min through now, capped at 24 h; no incident time: last 3 h. Mode B: last 7 days.
     58	- **Web ACL:** every ACL on the resources in the request; none identifiable: all ACLs (both scopes), top 3 by denying volume.
     59	- **Several tables or log groups:** the exact location match with the newest data.
     60	- **S3 logging but no table, or no logging:** don't stop; take the degraded path and report the gap with the advisory fix.
     61	- **Missing permission:** fall back to the next source and name the permission.
     62	
     63	## Discover
     64	
     65	Read [discovery-and-log-sources.md](references/discovery-and-log-sources.md) for D-1 to D-7 at the start of every run. Never ask for a resource or ACL.
     66	
     67	- **D-1 Resource to Web ACL:** CloudFront `GetDistributionConfig` `WebACLId`; regional resources `wafv2:GetWebACLForResource`.
     68	- **D-2 Read the ACL:** `wafv2:GetWebACL` for rule order, actions, managed groups and versions, `RuleActionOverrides`, Count overrides, scope-downs, custom responses, token domains, immunity times, and any `ShieldMitigationRuleGroup_*` rule.
     69	- **D-2b Token posture:** classify P0 (no token-aware rules), P1 (token labels, no or only threshold-based enforcement) or P2 (strict token enforcement); confirm with Q-18.
     70	- **D-3 Log destination:** `wafv2:GetLoggingConfiguration`, including logging filters and redacted fields. Log group: Logs Insights. S3 or Firehose to S3: Athena. None, or a non-S3 destination without a full S3 backup: degraded path.
     71	- **D-4 Find the table or log group:** list tables in **every** Glue database, including `default`, across the Regions in D-4. Write "no table" only after that full listing. Never analyze raw log objects (`s3:GetObject`) as a substitute.
     72	- **D-7 Shield Advanced status:** `shield:DescribeSubscription`, `DescribeProtection` (L7AM status and action), `ListAttacks`/`DescribeAttack`, and `DDoSDetected` in `AWS/DDoSProtection`.
     73	
     74	**Region rule.** For CloudFront scope, the ACL, its logging configuration, its log group and its `AWS/WAFV2` metrics are in us-east-1. Only the Glue table and Athena follow the customer's setup; run Athena in the table's Region.
     75	
     76	## Bind schema and guard cost
     77	
     78	Queries are cited as `Q-NN (QA-NN / QI-NN)`. Run the one that matches the backend from D-3 and D-4. Read "Schema binding and cost guards (detail)" in [discovery-and-log-sources.md](references/discovery-and-log-sources.md) when you bind placeholders or brief the log subagent.
     79	
     80	- **Athena:** bind `<table>`, `<req>`, label type and `<pf>` from `glue:GetTable`. The log subagent reads [athena-queries.md](references/athena-queries.md) "Schema binding" and the query sections it runs.
     81	- **Logs Insights:** the log subagent reads [logs-insights-queries.md](references/logs-insights-queries.md) "Conventions" and the query sections it runs.
     82	- **Probe first, in the log subagent.** The main agent runs no Athena query. On a probe error, take the degraded path.
     83	- **Cost:** prune partitions, start narrow, no unbounded `SELECT *`, at most one `UNNEST` per query.
     84	- **Budget:** about 15 log queries (about 10 on the Mode B fast path). Report queries run and bytes scanned.
     85	
     86	## Run it in AWS DevOps Agent
     87	
     88	The main agent discovers; subagents query. Read "Subagent briefs" in [discovery-and-log-sources.md](references/discovery-and-log-sources.md) before you start a log subagent, and when your prompt says discovery is done.
     89	
     90	**If your prompt says discovery is done and you are a subagent:** skip Steps 1 to 3, start no further subagents and do not load this skill again. Follow "Subagent briefs" for your role.
     91	
     92	**If you are a subagent without a discovery brief** (the platform handed you the whole task, so no main agent ran Steps 1 to 3): do the main agent's and the log subagent's work yourself, and start no further log subagent.
     93	
     94	1. Do D-1 to D-4. For D-4, call `glue:GetTables` on every database that `glue:GetDatabases` returns, including `default`, and match `Location` to the log prefix. A database list alone never means "no table".
     95	2. Never download raw S3 log objects to analyze them. Never use sampled requests for a window that ends more than 3 hours ago.
     96	3. Run the probe, then the mode's queries. Copy each query verbatim from [athena-queries.md](references/athena-queries.md) or [logs-insights-queries.md](references/logs-insights-queries.md) by searching for its ID (for example `QA-13b`). Never summarize the query references with a distill tool: summaries drop mandatory queries.
     97	4. In Mode B, run Q-13b and Q-19 whatever else you run.
     98	5. Return the full Output block, so the agent that started you can pass it on verbatim.
     99	
     100	- [ ] Step 1: **Main agent: discover, bind, delegate.**
     101	  - Load this skill once. Load no other log-search or log-analysis skill.
     102	  - Read reference sections by search or offset, not whole files.
     103	  - Do D-1 to D-4, D-2b and `glue:GetTable` (or find the log group) yourself.
     104	  - Start **one** log-analysis subagent with `preloaded_skills: ['aws-waf-log-analysis']` where supported.
     105	  - Start the change subagent (Step 3) in the same turn, so both run concurrently.
     106	  - The brief carries everything bound, the mode and steps, the budget, and the return format. Keep it neutral. Give every launch a unique `name`.
     107	- [ ] Step 2: **Main agent: no query libraries, no log queries.** Do metrics (A1, D-5) and Shield (D-7) yourself while the subagent runs. At most one follow-up log pass, for a new uncharacterized candidate; never a third pass.
     108	- [ ] Step 3: **CloudTrail only in a change subagent, never in the main agent.**
     109	  - Every `cloudtrail:LookupEvents` (A5; "After `WAF_CLEARED`"; Mode B change correlation) runs in one change subagent.
     110	  - Launch: `agent_type` `generic`, `name` `change-timeline`, `preloaded_skills: ['aws-waf-log-analysis', 'investigating-infrastructure-changes']` (whichever are available).
     111	  - Always start it, even when memory or an earlier refusal says CloudTrail is blocked. It is mandatory for a rule-out request.
     112	  - Its prompt points it to "Change lookups" in [access-denied-triage.md](references/access-denied-triage.md), which holds the Regions, event names, sweep and return contract.
     113	  - Write "blocked" or "denied" only on the change subagent's own `AccessDenied`.
     114	  - No completed lookup: write "changes: not checked (<reason>)". Never "no change", "ruled out" or "CloudTrail is blocked in this environment".
     115	- [ ] Step 4: **Subagents return compact aggregates only.** Per query: ID, row count, bytes scanned, about 20 top rows. Payloads as class and count only. Never raw result sets or whole log records.
     116	- [ ] Step 5: **Refusal, failure or no subagent capability.**
     117	  - Relaunch a refused log or change subagent once, under a new name, with the same `preloaded_skills`.
     118	  - Change relaunch fails too: "changes: not checked (change subagent refused twice)".
     119	  - Log relaunch fails too, or no subagents: run about 10 count-only aggregate queries yourself and record the fallback.
     120	  - A3/A4 detail is then out of reach: say so and cap confidence at "low".
     121	
     122	## Rule and label knowledge
     123	
     124	Read L-1 in [label-reference.md](references/label-reference.md) when you need a rule or label meaning (in AWS DevOps Agent, inside the log subagent).
     125	
     126	- Order: `wafv2:DescribeManagedRuleGroup` with the ACL's version when permitted (opt-in; record a denial). Then exact label strings from Q-09 (casing can differ from rule names). Then the bundled, dated tables.
     127	- A connected AWS documentation tool may confirm semantics but is never required.
     128	- A label found in neither the API output nor the bundled tables is "meaning unverified". Never infer meaning from its name.
     129	
     130	## Mode A: access-denied triage
     131	
     132	Read [access-denied-triage.md](references/access-denied-triage.md) when Mode A runs; it holds the detail of each step. Read [remediation-patterns.md](references/remediation-patterns.md) (R-01 to R-11) at Step A7.
     133	
     134	- [ ] Step A0: **WAF rule-out**, cheapest first: Web ACL in the path; symptom type fits WAF; denying metrics and Shield or Anti-DDoS signals rose; Q-15 shows denials on the scope.
     135	  - Wording alone never clears WAF (a 202 with an empty body is often reported as "timeout").
     136	  - Only "no Web ACL in the path" stops the WAF checks at once. The change subagent still runs the origin-side checks.
     137	  - After `WAF_CLEARED`, list origin-side next steps as checks, not conclusions. Name no root cause outside WAF that evidence does not show.
     138	  - When the change subagent finds an origin-side change whose time matches onset and recovery, record it as the Root Cause with the event evidence and the load-balancer metrics; never stop at "out of scope".
     139	- [ ] Step A1: **Confirm involvement:** front-door 4xx versus `AWS/WAFV2` Blocked/Challenge/Captcha per rule, against the preceding window and the prior day, with request-volume stability. Never clear WAF on 4xx alone.
     140	- [ ] Step A2: **Attribute:** group terminating records by action, rule, managed sub-rule, response code and time bucket (Q-02, Q-01, Q-14 for Shield L7AM).
     141	- [ ] Step A3: **Client capability (Challenge/CAPTCHA only):** token posture and the path's token-status profile (Q-18, Q-05, Q-09, Q-04). Quote the `failureReason` value with its count (for example `TOKEN_MISSING`).
     142	- [ ] Step A4: **Profile who is affected:** clients, URIs and match details against allowed history before onset (Q-03, Q-04, Q-06, Q-07, Q-10, Q-12, Q-13). For blocked attackers, run Q-19; never "benign" without it.
     143	- [ ] Step A5: **Correlate changes and events:** CloudTrail (change subagent), managed group versions, Anti-DDoS `event-detected` onset, Shield attacks (D-7). A version change or association is a cause only under the A5 evidence rules. No completed lookup: "changes: not checked".
     144	- [ ] Step A6: **Verdict** per denying (rule, action) pair: `FALSE_POSITIVE`, `CLIENT_CANNOT_SOLVE`, `CORRECT_MITIGATION` or `MIXED`; or overall `WAF_CLEARED` or `INCONCLUSIVE`. Give confidence (high, likely, low) and quantified impact.
     145	  - Missing allowed history is not evidence of attack. A monitor, health checker or integration with a benign profile hit by a header-presence or size rule is `FALSE_POSITIVE` (likely), with owner confirmation under "Verify before acting".
     146	- [ ] Step A7: **Advise:** the narrowest R-xx fix, marked *reduces* or *eliminates*, validated in Count first (straight to Block only as R-01's labelled alternative).
     147	  - `CLIENT_CANNOT_SOLVE`: first a path scope-down of the challenge rule (R-05, covering every observed non-HTML path, including `/`), or token/SDK integration (R-06). Both rank above R-04.
     148	  - An IP or path is only a scope-down or exclusion on the challenge rule itself. Never add the client to an IP set used by an Allow-action rule.
     149	  - Never offer removing or disabling the Web ACL.
     150	
     151	## Mode B: threat hunting
     152	
     153	Read [threat-hunting.md](references/threat-hunting.md) when Mode B runs, and classify with [threat-taxonomy.md](references/threat-taxonomy.md) at Step B6. Detected-not-blocked is a priority finding (threat labels on ALLOW, Count-mode matches, rate rules in Count, attacker residue). If the logging filter drops ALLOW records, say the analysis is limited.
     154	
     155	- [ ] Step B1: **Fast path first** for a window of 2 hours or less, or one specific question: about 10 fixed queries, started together, polled once. The full set is in "Fast path".
     156	  - Q-13b is mandatory. It sets the top talker apart so a short burst cannot hide.
     157	  - Every sensitive-path burst and every client over a rate-rule limit is a finding with method, URI, count, peaks and first to last seen. Never "ordinary", "normal" or "a retry burst".
     158	  - Run the full funnel only for candidates the fast path cannot settle.
     159	- [ ] Step B2: **B0 Known automation:** high-volume, low-diversity clients with corroboration, excluded from baselines (Q-13, Q-12, Q-01). Report them under a required "Known automation" heading. Never label them card testing or abuse. Never exclude a population with token-reuse or coordinated-activity labels.
     160	- [ ] Step B3: **B-A Overview and B-B Standouts:** time series, breakdowns and label frequency (Q-01, Q-02, Q-03, Q-09); then standouts ranked numerically (Q-08, Q-11, Q-12, Q-14, Q-16b, Q-17).
     161	- [ ] Step B4: **Attacker residue (B-B):** for every client with any BLOCK from an injection, bad-input or bot rule, report its ALLOW requests as a missed-by-rule finding (Q-19).
     162	  - Never "benign", "clean" or "accounted for" unless Q-19 showed `args_class` `none` on application paths.
     163	  - Explain a miss only from the rule's documented inspection target (L-1); otherwise "reason not determined".
     164	  - Copy the field location verbatim. A query-argument residue needs a query-string rule; a `UriPath` rule does not cover it.
     165	- [ ] Step B5: **B-C to B-E Drill, narrow, confirm:** re-pivot one standout; one line per Count or rate-rule client (Q-08c); narrow to one client, rule or endpoint; confirm with Q-10 or Q-16b/Q-16.
     166	  - A burst on a payment, checkout, login, signup or password-reset URI is a card-testing or credential-stuffing finding whatever its size. Fix it with a path-scoped R-10 on that URI, Count first.
     167	- [ ] Step B6: **B-F and B-G:** resolve load-bearing labels (L-1; unverified stays unverified), map each signature to a class and an R-xx mitigation, and hand legitimate-user denials to Mode A.
     168	- [ ] Step B7: **Record, then generate the hunting report.** Write the Mode B records first ("Records" under "Output"). If the runtime can create a report artifact, write the hunting report as a Markdown artifact. Before writing it, load the report template, [assets/threat-hunt-report-template.md](assets/threat-hunt-report-template.md), and follow its section order and tables exactly:
     169	  ```
     170	  read_skill_resource(skill_id="aws-waf-log-analysis", path="assets/threat-hunt-report-template.md")
     171	  ```
     172	  - The investigation records remain the primary deliverable; the report repeats their numbers and never adds a finding they lack.
     173	  - No artifact capability: put the same sections into the final message, after the Output template block.
     174	  - **If the `read_skill_resource` call fails**, note at the top of the report "report template (`assets/threat-hunt-report-template.md`) could not be loaded; structure follows the Mode B contract", and still produce the sections of "Output (Mode B contract)" in [threat-hunting.md](references/threat-hunting.md).
     175	
     176	## Degraded path
     177	
     178	Use when WAF logs can't be queried (no table, no logging, a non-S3 destination, or a missing permission). The investigation always continues. Read D-5 in [discovery-and-log-sources.md](references/discovery-and-log-sources.md) when you take this path.
     179	
     180	- **WAF metrics** say *whether* WAF denied and *which rule*, not *who* or *which path*.
     181	- **Sampled requests:** last 3 hours only, examples rather than counts.
     182	- **Confidence:** cap at "likely" (A0 structural clears can be high). With Shield L7AM attached, a metric-based clear is `INCONCLUSIVE`. Lower to "low" when A3 or A4 cannot be assessed.
     183	- **Wrap-up:** state that WAF logs weren't analyzed and why, with the advisory fix (D-6 DDL, logging configuration, or the missing permission).
     184

   - AWSManagedRulesKnownBadInputsRuleSet / Log4JRCE_HEADER (×15)
   Payload classes: sqli ×90 (query args + body), xss ×60 (query args), traversal-lfi ×30 (query args), ssrf ×15 (query args), cmd-rce/log4j ×15 (HTTP header).
2. DETECTED-NOT-BLOCKED / MISSED-BY-RULE (high): 15 traversal-lfi requests from the same client 198.51.100.40 to URI /catalog were ALLOWED through to the origin. Field location: URI path / query argument. No managed sub-rule matched these 15, although GenericLFI_QUERYARGUMENTS blocked 30 other LFI attempts from the same client. Miss reason not fully determined from logs — likely the traversal landed in a component/location the matched GenericLFI query-args sub-rule did not inspect; confirm against the sub-rule's documented inspection target.
3. DETECTED-NOT-BLOCKED / RATE RULE IN COUNT (high): AWS-RateBasedRule-IP-300-CreatedByCloudFront (300 req / 300s per IP, AggregateKeyType IP) is in COUNT. It matched 56,232 requests in the window and blocked none. The ONLY client over the limit is benign known automation — the Artillery load-testing tool at 198.51.100.10 (UA "Artillery (https://artillery.io)", 99.6% of traffic, peak 11,924 req / 5 min, ~40× the limit, all ALLOW, no threat labels).

CHOSEN REMEDIATION PATTERNS (from the skill's remediation-patterns.md R-xx; propose precise, scoped, Count-first versions):
- WAF layer: add a query-string / URI-path LFI-traversal rule (custom rule or appropriate managed sub-rule) covering /catalog and all application paths to catch the traversal-lfi residue that GenericLFI missed (R-01/R-02 pattern). Validate in Count before Block. For 198.51.100.40 specifically, a path-scoped Count→Block on the matched injection signatures is acceptable.
- Rate rule: the site-wide rate-based rule MUST stay in COUNT — a site-wide flip to Block would block the Artillery load tool (~40× over the limit) and any shared-egress clients (R-10). If enforcement is desired, scope a rate rule to exclude the known load-test source (198.51.100.10) or to sensitive paths only, Count first.
- Application layer: confirm /catalog origin handling rejects/escapes path-traversal input independently of WAF (R-11).

HARD CONSTRAINTS (per the aws-waf-log-analysis mitigation handoff):
- Scope every fix to the affected path, method, rule, or client. Count first before any Block.
- NEVER recommend a site-wide Block on the rate-based rule while known automation / shared egress exceeds the limit.
- NEVER disable, delete, or blanket-Count-override a rule group, and NEVER remove or disassociate the Web ACL.
- NEVER add any client to an IP set used by an Allow-action rule.
- Split WAF-layer and application-layer measures. Advisory only — do not apply.

     22	
     23	# AWS WAF Log Analysis
     24	
     25	Find out whether AWS WAF (including Anti-DDoS rules and Shield Advanced automatic mitigation) is denying legitimate traffic (Mode A). Or hunt WAF logs for threats, including what WAF detected but did not block (Mode B).
     26	
     27	## Purpose and guarantees
     28	
     29	- **Read-only.** Use only Describe, Get and List calls, plus `logs:StartQuery`/`GetQueryResults`, `athena:StartQueryExecution` (SELECT only, when permitted)/`GetQueryResults`, `cloudtrail:LookupEvents`, `wafv2:GetSampledRequests` and `cloudwatch:GetMetricData`.
     30	- Never run DDL. Never change a Web ACL, rule, IP set, Shield setting, log configuration or any other resource.
     31	- **Advisory.** Describe fixes in prose for a human to review and apply. Never apply them.
     32	- **Single-turn.** Never ask the user a question and never wait for input. Apply "Defaults when input is missing", record every default under "Assumptions", and continue.
     33	- **Never stop on a gap.** A denied call or a missing table moves you to the next source or the degraded path. It does not end the investigation.
     34	- **Exact errors.** Record the exact error code. Call something "not permitted" only on `AccessDenied`/`UnauthorizedOperation`.
     35	  - A cancelled, timed-out or throttled call is retried once, then reported as not completed.
     36	  - A tool refusal such as "service operations are not allowed" means: run the call in a subagent.
     37	- **Records are the deliverable.** In both modes the investigation records (symptoms, observations, findings, gaps, hypotheses) are what is judged and shown; the last message closes them (see "Output").
     38	- **Final output.** The answer is complete as delivered. It never ends with a question or an offer. Never call `ask_user` (or any ask tool), not even after the answer to offer follow-up work or a fix: a turn that ends on a tool call loses the answer. Put follow-ups in "Next steps" and end on plain text.
     39	
     40	## Pick the mode from the request
     41	
     42	Inputs are the investigation request text, plus any attached incident or alarm details (alarm name, metric, resource, start time). A threat hunt needs no alarm: a user-requested investigation with hunting language is Mode B. Classify, and record the choice under "Assumptions".
     43	
     44	| Request contains | Mode |
     45	|---|---|
     46	| Denial or error symptoms: 403/405/202, "blocked", "can't access", "unreachable", "partner integration failing", a 4xx/5xx spike, timeouts, or an alarm on a front-door resource | **Mode A**, starting with the A0 rule-out |
     47	| Hunting language: "malicious", "scan", "attack", "bots", "is WAF missing anything", "review WAF logs", a scheduled or recurring review | **Mode B** |
     48	| Both | Mode A first, then Mode B on the same window, focused on the slice Mode A found |
     49	| Neither, but the incident involves a resource that a Web ACL protects | **A0 rule-out only**; if A0 finds WAF implicated or inconclusive, continue with A1 to A7 |
     50	
     51	When Mode A's verdict is `CORRECT_MITIGATION` (a real attack), recommend Mode B on that slice. Run it in the same investigation when the request is in scope for hunting.
     52	
     53	## Defaults when input is missing
     54	
     55	Never ask. Apply the default and record it. Read "Defaults when input is missing (full table)" in [discovery-and-log-sources.md](references/discovery-and-log-sources.md) when an input below is missing and you need the exact fallback.
     56	
     57	- **Time window:** Mode A: incident start minus 30 min through now, capped at 24 h; no incident time: last 3 h. Mode B: last 7 days.
     58	- **Web ACL:** every ACL on the resources in the request; none identifiable: all ACLs (both scopes), top 3 by denying volume.
     59	- **Several tables or log groups:** the exact location match with the newest data.
     60	- **S3 logging but no table, or no logging:** don't stop; take the degraded path and report the gap with the advisory fix.
     61	- **Missing permission:** fall back to the next source and name the permission.
     62	
     63	## Discover
     64	
     65	Read [discovery-and-log-sources.md](references/discovery-and-log-sources.md) for D-1 to D-7 at the start of every run. Never ask for a resource or ACL.
     66	
     67	- **D-1 Resource to Web ACL:** CloudFront `GetDistributionConfig` `WebACLId`; regional resources `wafv2:GetWebACLForResource`.
     68	- **D-2 Read the ACL:** `wafv2:GetWebACL` for rule order, actions, managed groups and versions, `RuleActionOverrides`, Count overrides, scope-downs, custom responses, token domains, immunity times, and any `ShieldMitigationRuleGroup_*` rule.
     69	- **D-2b Token posture:** classify P0 (no token-aware rules), P1 (token labels, no or only threshold-based enforcement) or P2 (strict token enforcement); confirm with Q-18.
     70	- **D-3 Log destination:** `wafv2:GetLoggingConfiguration`, including logging filters and redacted fields. Log group: Logs Insights. S3 or Firehose to S3: Athena. None, or a non-S3 destination without a full S3 backup: degraded path.
     71	- **D-4 Find the table or log group:** list tables in **every** Glue database, including `default`, across the Regions in D-4. Write "no table" only after that full listing. Never analyze raw log objects (`s3:GetObject`) as a substitute.
     72	- **D-7 Shield Advanced status:** `shield:DescribeSubscription`, `DescribeProtection` (L7AM status and action), `ListAttacks`/`DescribeAttack`, and `DDoSDetected` in `AWS/DDoSProtection`.
     73	
     74	**Region rule.** For CloudFront scope, the ACL, its logging configuration, its log group and its `AWS/WAFV2` metrics are in us-east-1. Only the Glue table and Athena follow the customer's setup; run Athena in the table's Region.
     75	
     76	## Bind schema and guard cost
     77	
     78	Queries are cited as `Q-NN (QA-NN / QI-NN)`. Run the one that matches the backend from D-3 and D-4. Read "Schema binding and cost guards (detail)" in [discovery-and-log-sources.md](references/discovery-and-log-sources.md) when you bind placeholders or brief the log subagent.
     79	
     80	- **Athena:** bind `<table>`, `<req>`, label type and `<pf>` from `glue:GetTable`. The log subagent reads [athena-queries.md](references/athena-queries.md) "Schema binding" and the query sections it runs.
     81	- **Logs Insights:** the log subagent reads [logs-insights-queries.md](references/logs-insights-queries.md) "Conventions" and the query sections it runs.
     82	- **Probe first, in the log subagent.** The main agent runs no Athena query. On a probe error, take the degraded path.
     83	- **Cost:** prune partitions, start narrow, no unbounded `SELECT *`, at most one `UNNEST` per query.
     84	- **Budget:** about 15 log queries (about 10 on the Mode B fast path). Report queries run and bytes scanned.
     85	
     86	## Run it in AWS DevOps Agent
     87	
     88	The main agent discovers; subagents query. Read "Subagent briefs" in [discovery-and-log-sources.md](references/discovery-and-log-sources.md) before you start a log subagent, and when your prompt says discovery is done.
     89	
     90	**If your prompt says discovery is done and you are a subagent:** skip Steps 1 to 3, start no further subagents and do not load this skill again. Follow "Subagent briefs" for your role.
     91	
     92	**If you are a subagent without a discovery brief** (the platform handed you the whole task, so no main agent ran Steps 1 to 3): do the main agent's and the log subagent's work yourself, and start no further log subagent.
     93	
     94	1. Do D-1 to D-4. For D-4, call `glue:GetTables` on every database that `glue:GetDatabases` returns, including `default`, and match `Location` to the log prefix. A database list alone never means "no table".
     95	2. Never download raw S3 log objects to analyze them. Never use sampled requests for a window that ends more than 3 hours ago.
     96	3. Run the probe, then the mode's queries. Copy each query verbatim from [athena-queries.md](references/athena-queries.md) or [logs-insights-queries.md](references/logs-insights-queries.md) by searching for its ID (for example `QA-13b`). Never summarize the query references with a distill tool: summaries drop mandatory queries.
     97	4. In Mode B, run Q-13b and Q-19 whatever else you run.
     98	5. Return the full Output block, so the agent that started you can pass it on verbatim.
     99	
     100	- [ ] Step 1: **Main agent: discover, bind, delegate.**
     101	  - Load this skill once. Load no other log-search or log-analysis skill.
     102	  - Read reference sections by search or offset, not whole files.
     103	  - Do D-1 to D-4, D-2b and `glue:GetTable` (or find the log group) yourself.
     104	  - Start **one** log-analysis subagent with `preloaded_skills: ['aws-waf-log-analysis']` where supported.
     105	  - Start the change subagent (Step 3) in the same turn, so both run concurrently.
     106	  - The brief carries everything bound, the mode and steps, the budget, and the return format. Keep it neutral. Give every launch a unique `name`.
     107	- [ ] Step 2: **Main agent: no query libraries, no log queries.** Do metrics (A1, D-5) and Shield (D-7) yourself while the subagent runs. At most one follow-up log pass, for a new uncharacterized candidate; never a third pass.
     108	- [ ] Step 3: **CloudTrail only in a change subagent, never in the main agent.**
     109	  - Every `cloudtrail:LookupEvents` (A5; "After `WAF_CLEARED`"; Mode B change correlation) runs in one change subagent.
     110	  - Launch: `agent_type` `generic`, `name` `change-timeline`, `preloaded_skills: ['aws-waf-log-analysis', 'investigating-infrastructure-changes']` (whichever are available).
     111	  - Always start it, even when memory or an earlier refusal says CloudTrail is blocked. It is mandatory for a rule-out request.
     112	  - Its prompt points it to "Change lookups" in [access-denied-triage.md](references/access-denied-triage.md), which holds the Regions, event names, sweep and return contract.
     113	  - Write "blocked" or "denied" only on the change subagent's own `AccessDenied`.
     114	  - No completed lookup: write "changes: not checked (<reason>)". Never "no change", "ruled out" or "CloudTrail is blocked in this environment".
     115	- [ ] Step 4: **Subagents return compact aggregates only.** Per query: ID, row count, bytes scanned, about 20 top rows. Payloads as class and count only. Never raw result sets or whole log records.
     116	- [ ] Step 5: **Refusal, failure or no subagent capability.**
     117	  - Relaunch a refused log or change subagent once, under a new name, with the same `preloaded_skills`.
     118	  - Change relaunch fails too: "changes: not checked (change subagent refused twice)".
     119	  - Log relaunch fails too, or no subagents: run about 10 count-only aggregate queries yourself and record the fallback.
     120	  - A3/A4 detail is then out of reach: say so and cap confidence at "low".
     121	
     122	## Rule and label knowledge
     123	
     124	Read L-1 in [label-reference.md](references/label-reference.md) when you need a rule or label meaning (in AWS DevOps Agent, inside the log subagent).
     125	
     126	- Order: `wafv2:DescribeManagedRuleGroup` with the ACL's version when permitted (opt-in; record a denial). Then exact label strings from Q-09 (casing can differ from rule names). Then the bundled, dated tables.
     127	- A connected AWS documentation tool may confirm semantics but is never required.
     128	- A label found in neither the API output nor the bundled tables is "meaning unverified". Never infer meaning from its name.
     129	
     130	## Mode A: access-denied triage
     131	
     132	Read [access-denied-triage.md](references/access-denied-triage.md) when Mode A runs; it holds the detail of each step. Read [remediation-patterns.md](references/remediation-patterns.md) (R-01 to R-11) at Step A7.
     133	
     134	- [ ] Step A0: **WAF rule-out**, cheapest first: Web ACL in the path; symptom type fits WAF; denying metrics and Shield or Anti-DDoS signals rose; Q-15 shows denials on the scope.
     135	  - Wording alone never clears WAF (a 202 with an empty body is often reported as "timeout").
     136	  - Only "no Web ACL in the path" stops the WAF checks at once. The change subagent still runs the origin-side checks.
     137	  - After `WAF_CLEARED`, list origin-side next steps as checks, not conclusions. Name no root cause outside WAF that evidence does not show.
     138	  - When the change subagent finds an origin-side change whose time matches onset and recovery, record it as the Root Cause with the event evidence and the load-balancer metrics; never stop at "out of scope".
     139	- [ ] Step A1: **Confirm involvement:** front-door 4xx versus `AWS/WAFV2` Blocked/Challenge/Captcha per rule, against the preceding window and the prior day, with request-volume stability. Never clear WAF on 4xx alone.
     140	- [ ] Step A2: **Attribute:** group terminating records by action, rule, managed sub-rule, response code and time bucket (Q-02, Q-01, Q-14 for Shield L7AM).
     141	- [ ] Step A3: **Client capability (Challenge/CAPTCHA only):** token posture and the path's token-status profile (Q-18, Q-05, Q-09, Q-04). Quote the `failureReason` value with its count (for example `TOKEN_MISSING`).
     142	- [ ] Step A4: **Profile who is affected:** clients, URIs and match details against allowed history before onset (Q-03, Q-04, Q-06, Q-07, Q-10, Q-12, Q-13). For blocked attackers, run Q-19; never "benign" without it.
     143	- [ ] Step A5: **Correlate changes and events:** CloudTrail (change subagent), managed group versions, Anti-DDoS `event-detected` onset, Shield attacks (D-7). A version change or association is a cause only under the A5 evidence rules. No completed lookup: "changes: not checked".
     144	- [ ] Step A6: **Verdict** per denying (rule, action) pair: `FALSE_POSITIVE`, `CLIENT_CANNOT_SOLVE`, `CORRECT_MITIGATION` or `MIXED`; or overall `WAF_CLEARED` or `INCONCLUSIVE`. Give confidence (high, likely, low) and quantified impact.
     145	  - Missing allowed history is not evidence of attack. A monitor, health checker or integration with a benign profile hit by a header-presence or size rule is `FALSE_POSITIVE` (likely), with owner confirmation under "Verify before acting".
     146	- [ ] Step A7: **Advise:** the narrowest R-xx fix, marked *reduces* or *eliminates*, validated in Count first (straight to Block only as R-01's labelled alternative).
     147	  - `CLIENT_CANNOT_SOLVE`: first a path scope-down of the challenge rule (R-05, covering every observed non-HTML path, including `/`), or token/SDK integration (R-06). Both rank above R-04.
     148	  - An IP or path is only a scope-down or exclusion on the challenge rule itself. Never add the client to an IP set used by an Allow-action rule.
     149	  - Never offer removing or disabling the Web ACL.
     150	
     151	## Mode B: threat hunting
     152	
     153	Read [threat-hunting.md](references/threat-hunting.md) when Mode B runs, and classify with [threat-taxonomy.md](references/threat-taxonomy.md) at Step B6. Detected-not-blocked is a priority finding (threat labels on ALLOW, Count-mode matches, rate rules in Count, attacker residue). If the logging filter drops ALLOW records, say the analysis is limited.
     154	
     155	- [ ] Step B1: **Fast path first** for a window of 2 hours or less, or one specific question: about 10 fixed queries, started together, polled once. The full set is in "Fast path".
     156	  - Q-13b is mandatory. It sets the top talker apart so a short burst cannot hide.
     157	  - Every sensitive-path burst and every client over a rate-rule limit is a finding with method, URI, count, peaks and first to last seen. Never "ordinary", "normal" or "a retry burst".
     158	  - Run the full funnel only for candidates the fast path cannot settle.
     159	- [ ] Step B2: **B0 Known automation:** high-volume, low-diversity clients with corroboration, excluded from baselines (Q-13, Q-12, Q-01). Report them under a required "Known automation" heading. Never label them card testing or abuse. Never exclude a population with token-reuse or coordinated-activity labels.
     160	- [ ] Step B3: **B-A Overview and B-B Standouts:** time series, breakdowns and label frequency (Q-01, Q-02, Q-03, Q-09); then standouts ranked numerically (Q-08, Q-11, Q-12, Q-14, Q-16b, Q-17).
     161	- [ ] Step B4: **Attacker residue (B-B):** for every client with any BLOCK from an injection, bad-input or bot rule, report its ALLOW requests as a missed-by-rule finding (Q-19).
     162	  - Never "benign", "clean" or "accounted for" unless Q-19 showed `args_class` `none` on application paths.
     163	  - Explain a miss only from the rule's documented inspection target (L-1); otherwise "reason not determined".
     164	  - Copy the field location verbatim. A query-argument residue needs a query-string rule; a `UriPath` rule does not cover it.
     165	- [ ] Step B5: **B-C to B-E Drill, narrow, confirm:** re-pivot one standout; one line per Count or rate-rule client (Q-08c); narrow to one client, rule or endpoint; confirm with Q-10 or Q-16b/Q-16.
     166	  - A burst on a payment, checkout, login, signup or password-reset URI is a card-testing or credential-stuffing finding whatever its size. Fix it with a path-scoped R-10 on that URI, Count first.
     167	- [ ] Step B6: **B-F and B-G:** resolve load-bearing labels (L-1; unverified stays unverified), map each signature to a class and an R-xx mitigation, and hand legitimate-user denials to Mode A.
     168	- [ ] Step B7: **Record, then generate the hunting report.** Write the Mode B records first ("Records" under "Output"). If the runtime can create a report artifact, write the hunting report as a Markdown artifact. Before writing it, load the report template, [assets/threat-hunt-report-template.md](assets/threat-hunt-report-template.md), and follow its section order and tables exactly:
     169	  ```
     170	  read_skill_resource(skill_id="aws-waf-log-analysis", path="assets/threat-hunt-report-template.md")
     171	  ```
     172	  - The investigation records remain the primary deliverable; the report repeats their numbers and never adds a finding they lack.
     173	  - No artifact capability: put the same sections into the final message, after the Output template block.
     174	  - **If the `read_skill_resource` call fails**, note at the top of the report "report template (`assets/threat-hunt-report-template.md`) could not be loaded; structure follows the Mode B contract", and still produce the sections of "Output (Mode B contract)" in [threat-hunting.md](references/threat-hunting.md).
     175	
     176	## Degraded path
     177	
     178	Use when WAF logs can't be queried (no table, no logging, a non-S3 destination, or a missing permission). The investigation always continues. Read D-5 in [discovery-and-log-sources.md](references/discovery-and-log-sources.md) when you take this path.
     179	
     180	- **WAF metrics** say *whether* WAF denied and *which rule*, not *who* or *which path*.
     181	- **Sampled requests:** last 3 hours only, examples rather than counts.
     182	- **Confidence:** cap at "likely" (A0 structural clears can be high). With Shield L7AM attached, a metric-based clear is `INCONCLUSIVE`. Lower to "low" when A3 or A4 cannot be assessed.
     183	- **Wrap-up:** state that WAF logs weren't analyzed and why, with the advisory fix (D-6 DDL, logging configuration, or the missing permission).
     184	
     185	## Output
     186	
     187	Read [output-contract.md](references/output-contract.md) before you write any record, handoff or final answer. It holds the record rules for both modes, the last-message rules and the mitigation handoff text. The mode sections are in the mode references.
     188	
     189	**Template.** The main agent's very last message closes the investigation, in every mode and verdict, including any reply after the mitigation step. It starts with `Assumptions:` (no preface) and repeats this block even if earlier messages carried it:
     190	
     191	```
     192	Assumptions: window; Web ACLs; backend; mode; defaults, fallbacks, calls not completed (exact error)
     193	Verdict: <Mode A: per (rule, action), or WAF_CLEARED / INCONCLUSIVE; Mode B: per confirmed finding> (confidence: high | likely | low)
     194	Evidence: <key numbers from the log subagent's table (step-5 fallback: your recorded results), with query IDs>; Changes (CloudTrail): <per category, Regions/sources/names searched: events found | none found>; origin-side: not checked (<reason>) if not searched | not checked (<reason>) | not applicable (Mode B)
     195	AI-generated: findings need human verification before anyone acts on them.
     196	```
     197	
     198	Then the mode sections, the findings, the next steps, and a last line `Ruled out: <each hypothesis, with the evidence that closed it, or "still open">`.
     199	
     200	**Counts.** Copy every count from the log subagent's table; never recompute or round. Memory about earlier incidents is never evidence.
     201	
     202	**Records.** Platform records are the judged deliverable in both modes. In both:
     203	
     204	- one observation record per key result first (counts, window, baseline, query ID), so findings can cite them;
     205	- exactly one Root Cause;
     206	- every Cause and Root Cause finding lists those observation IDs in its supporting observations (never empty) and the Web ACL in its related resources;
     207	- a gap record per denied or not-completed call or unassessed step; closed hypotheses with their evidence.
     208	
     209	Mode A: one symptom per burst, with numbers; one Cause per denying (rule, action) pair, titled with the exact rule and sub-rule ID and the verdict.
     210	
     211	Mode B (full rules in "Mode B records" in [output-contract.md](references/output-contract.md)):
     212	
     213	- one Symptom per distinct activity pattern: window, client, method and path, counts;
     214	- one Cause per confirmed threat finding, titled with class, client and exact rule and sub-rule IDs, or "not matched by any rule", or "detected, not blocked: <rate rule> in Count";
     215	- known automation as an observation plus a closed hypothesis, never a threat finding;
     216	- the Root Cause is the overall assessment: what WAF caught, what it missed and why (for example a rate rule in Count), naming every Cause and linking their observations and any known-automation observation, with mitigations split WAF layer and Application layer (path-scoped R-10 first for card testing; when known automation exceeds the site-wide rate rule, one sentence that it stays in Count and why).
     217	
     218	**Mitigation guardrails** (every message, finding and handoff):
     219	
     220	- Never disable or remove a rule group or the Web ACL.

     223	- Never a site-wide rate-rule Block when known automation or shared egress exceeds the limit (R-10).

{"id": "26a1c312-354e-485c-8759-4bcef4fbbfe8", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_2eNeau585KrRjsPfq4qKaj", "content": [{"text": "     1	# Remediation Patterns (advisory)
     2	
     3	These patterns are the advice the agent gives in step A7 of `access-denied-triage.md` and in the advisory mitigations of Mode B. They are **advisory only**. The agent never applies them, never runs a command that changes a resource, and never presents a mutating CLI or API call. Describe the change in prose so that a human can review and apply it with their own change process.
     4	
     5	**How to present a pattern**
     6	
     7	- Pick the **narrowest** pattern that fixes the observed (rule, action) pair. Prefer scoping to one sub-rule, URI and method over a rule-group-wide change, and prefer any scoped change over an Allow.
     8	- Mark each pattern as **reduces** (lowers the impact or frequency but leaves part of the pattern) or **eliminates** (stops the observed pattern for the affected scope), for the specific finding.
     9	- Always include a **Count-first validation step**: deploy the new or changed rule in Count, watch its matches in logs (Q-08 (QA-08 / QI-08), QA-08b for rule-group sub-rules) and `CountedRequests` metrics for a representative period, then switch to the terminating action. A rule placed **after** a rule that blocks can never see the blocked requests (a terminating action ends evaluation), so a later label rule cannot be validated while the earlier sub-rule still blocks; use the label-rule sequence in R-01 for that case.
     10	- Name what a human should confirm before acting (for example, that the excluded client really is the partner, or that the excluded URI cannot carry attack payloads).
     11	- Never recommend loosening a rule for traffic judged `CORRECT_MITIGATION`. Never recommend turning a rule or rule group off as the fix (deleting it, removing it from the ACL, or a blanket Count override of a whole group), nor removing the Web ACL or disassociating it from a resource. Scoped sub-rule Count overrides paired with a label rule (R-01) and the R-08 options with their stated trade-off are allowed.
     12	- Use exact rule and label names as they appear in the logs or `GetWebACL`. Rule names and label names can differ in casing (rule `SizeRestrictions_BODY`, label `awswaf:managed:aws:core-rule-set:SizeRestrictions_Body`); copy labels from Q-09 (QA-09 / QI-09), never build them from rule IDs.
     13	
     14	| ID | Pattern | Typical verdict |
     15	|---|---|---|
     16	| R-01 | Override one managed sub-rule to Count, then block on its label with a scoped exception | `FALSE_POSITIVE` on one sub-rule |
     17	| R-02 | Size-rule exception for specific URIs | `FALSE_POSITIVE` on `SizeRestrictions_BODY` |
     18	| R-03 | Scope-down statement on the managed rule group | `FALSE_POSITIVE` for one known client |
     19	| R-04 | IP-based exception for a verified partner, scoped to the denying rule only (never an Allow rule) | `FALSE_POSITIVE` or `CLIENT_CANNOT_SOLVE` for a verified partner, last resort |
     20	| R-05 | Restrict Challenge/CAPTCHA to HTML GETs | `CLIENT_CANNOT_SOLVE` |
     21	| R-06 | Client integration (WAF JavaScript or mobile SDK) and `TokenDomains` | `CLIENT_CANNOT_SOLVE` |
     22	| R-07 | Block or rate-based rule instead of Challenge on machine-to-machine endpoints | `CLIENT_CANNOT_SOLVE` on API endpoints |
     23	| R-08 | Shield L7AM action to Count, or migrate to the Anti-DDoS managed rule group | `FALSE_POSITIVE` or `MIXED` from L7AM |
     24	| R-09 | Anti-DDoS rule group tuning | `CLIENT_CANNOT_SOLVE` or `MIXED` from Anti-DDoS |
     25	| R-10 | Rate-based rule from Count to scoped Block | abuse detected but not stopped |
     26	| R-11 | WAF-layer and application-layer mitigations for abuse | `CORRECT_MITIGATION` gaps, token abuse |
     27	
     28	---
     29	
     30	## R-01 - Override one managed sub-rule to Count, then block on its label with a scoped exception
     31	
     32	**When it applies:** one sub-rule of a managed rule group blocks legitimate requests on a well-defined scope (a URI, method, host or client), and the sub-rule is still valuable everywhere else.
     33	
     34	**Change (prose):** in the managed rule group reference, add a rule action override that sets only that sub-rule to Count. The sub-rule still adds its label to matching requests. Then add a custom rule **after** the rule group (higher priority number) whose statement is: the request has that sub-rule's label AND NOT (the scoped exception, for example URI path starts with the affected path and method is POST). Its action is Block (with the same custom response, if one was used). Requests outside the exception are still blocked exactly as before.
     35	
     36	**Effect:** eliminates the false positive inside the exception scope; protection elsewhere is unchanged. The exception scope itself loses that one sub-rule's protection, so keep it as narrow as possible.
     37	
     38	**Count-first validation (label-rule sequence):** a Block ends evaluation, so a label rule placed after the sub-rule never sees the requests the sub-rule blocks. Validate in this order:
     39	
     40	1. Override the sub-rule to Count. It stops blocking but still adds its label.
     41	2. Add the label rule with the scoped exception, with action Count. Deploy steps 1 and 2 in the same change.
     42	3. Over a representative window, compare the label rule's matches with all requests that carry the sub-rule's label (Q-08 (QA-08 / QI-08) and QA-08b for the sub-rule's Count matches, Q-09 (QA-09 / QI-09) for the label). The label rule should match every labelled request outside the exception and none inside it.
     43	4. Switch the label rule to Block.
     44	
     45	**Reduced-protection window:** between steps 1 and 4 the sub-rule's traffic is counted but not blocked anywhere. Keep that window short: deploy steps 1 and 2 together, use the shortest review window that still covers the application's normal traffic cycle, and schedule step 4 in advance. The Count-first sequence above is the recommendation.
     46	
     47	**Alternative (explicitly labelled, not the default): straight to Block.** When the exception is well understood (one exact path and method, confirmed from Q-03 and Q-04), a human may choose to put the label rule straight into Block in the same change as step 1. This avoids the reduced-protection window, but the risk is that an error in the label rule's statement or exception scope blocks legitimate traffic, or lets attack traffic through, without a Count review first. If chosen, watch the label rule's `BlockedRequests` and the excluded path closely right after the change and be ready to roll back.
     48	
     49	---
     50	
     51	## R-02 - Size-rule exception for `SizeRestrictions_BODY` on specific URIs
     52	
     53	**When it applies:** `SizeRestrictions_BODY` in the Core rule set (`AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet`) blocks legitimate large bodies (forms, uploads, large JSON) on specific URIs, while the same clients' other requests are allowed.
     54	
     55	**Change (prose):** apply R-01 to `SizeRestrictions_BODY`: override it to Count, then add a custom rule after the group that blocks on its label (copy the exact label from the logs, for example `awswaf:managed:aws:core-rule-set:SizeRestrictions_Body`) AND NOT (URI path is the affected path AND method is the affected method). Optionally add your own size constraint for the excluded URI (a body-size statement with a limit that fits the application's real maximum) so that the exception does not accept bodies of any size.
     56	
     57	Also check `AssociationConfig.RequestBody` in the Web ACL (D-2). It sets how much of the body WAF inspects for each resource type; the CloudFront default inspection size is 16 KB, and limits differ by resource type. Compare with `requestBodySizeInspectedByWAF` and `oversizeFields` from Q-07 (QA-07 / QI-07): content beyond the inspection limit is not inspected by any rule, so raising the inspection limit (which can affect cost) or handling oversize content explicitly may matter for the excluded URI. Raising `AssociationConfig.RequestBody` does **not** change the `SizeRestrictions_BODY` threshold (8 KB) and never fixes this false positive by itself; it only affects content-inspection rules on the excluded URI.
     58	
     59	**Effect:** eliminates the false positive on the excluded URI and method; with your own size constraint, it reduces rather than removes size protection there.
     60	
     61	**Count-first validation:** follow R-01's label-rule sequence: override `SizeRestrictions_BODY` to Count and add the label rule (and any new size constraint) in Count in the same change; confirm the label rule matches all labelled oversize requests outside the excluded URI and method and none of the legitimate large submissions on it; then switch the label rule (and size constraint) to Block. Size protection is reduced site-wide between the override and the switch, so keep that window short. Count-first is the recommendation; going straight to Block is only the explicitly labelled alternative in R-01 (reduced-protection window), with the risk stated there.
     62	
     63	---
     64	
     65	## R-03 - Scope-down statement on the managed rule group to exclude a known client
     66	
     67	**When it applies:** a known, verified client (a partner, a monitoring service, a scheduled job) trips one or more rules in a managed group, and the client can be identified reliably.
     68	
     69	**Change (prose):** add a scope-down statement to the managed rule group reference so that the group evaluates only requests that are NOT from that client. Identify the client with an IP set of its documented egress addresses, or with a header the client controls (for example a shared secret header added by the partner, or a header added by an upstream proxy you own). Prefer the IP set when the addresses are stable; a header can be copied by anyone who learns it, so treat it as a weaker identifier and keep its value secret.
     70	
     71	**Effect:** eliminates the denial for that client. The excluded client gets none of the group's protection, so this is broader than R-01.
     72	
     73	**Count-first validation:** before changing the scope-down, add a Count rule that matches the same client condition and confirm in logs that it matches only the intended client's requests (Q-03 (QA-03 / QI-03) for that rule's population).
     74	
     75	---
     76	
     77	## R-04 - IP-based exception for a verified partner, scoped to the denying rule only (use with caution)
     78	
     79	**When it applies:** a partner with fixed, verified egress addresses keeps being denied by one rule, and narrower patterns (R-01, R-03, and for Challenge or CAPTCHA R-05, R-06 and a path scope-down) are not practical. For `CLIENT_CANNOT_SOLVE`, R-04 ranks below R-05, R-06 and the path scope-down of the challenge rule: list it last, if at all, and say why (egress addresses change, and the address loses that rule's protection).
     80	
     81	**Change (prose):** use the partner's verified addresses only as an exclusion on the rule that denies it: a scope-down statement on that Challenge, CAPTCHA or blocking rule (or on the managed group reference, R-03) of the form "NOT (source IP in <partner IP set>)", preferably combined with the partner's paths or host (for example "NOT (IP in set AND URI path starts with `/api/`)"), or a label-scoped rule that excludes the set (R-01). Every other rule keeps evaluating the partner's requests.
     82	
     83	**Never** add the client's address to an IP set that an Allow-action rule references (an existing "allow" or trusted-address set included), and never create such an Allow rule: Allow is terminating and ends evaluation, so every rule after it, including managed rule groups, rate-based rules, Bot Control, Anti-DDoS and Shield L7AM mitigation, is skipped for that address, and a compromised or shared address gets unrestricted access. When D-2 shows an existing Allow rule on an IP set, name it only to say the client must not be added to it.
     84	
     85	**Effect:** eliminates the denial by that one rule for the partner's addresses (and paths); all other protection stays.
     86	
     87	**Count-first validation:** first add the same match (IP set AND paths) as a Count rule and confirm it matches only the partner's traffic (correct addresses, expected paths). List under "Verify before acting" that a human should confirm with the partner that the address list is complete and owned by them, and review the set regularly.
     88	
     89	---
     90	
     91	## R-05 - Restrict Challenge/CAPTCHA to HTML GETs
     92	
     93	**When it applies:** a Challenge or CAPTCHA rule hits clients that cannot solve it: API calls, JSON requests, browser fetch/XHR, health checks, partner integrations. This is the first-ranked fix for `CLIENT_CANNOT_SOLVE` (with R-06 for clients you control), above any R-04 IP-based exception; never suggest adding the client to an IP set used by an Allow rule (R-04).
     94	
     95	**Change (prose):** narrow the Challenge or CAPTCHA rule (or add a scope-down statement to the rule group that applies it) so that it only applies when all of these hold: the URI path does not start with any API prefix the affected client uses (for example `/api/`, the first and simplest scope-down to name), the `Accept` header contains `text/html`, and the method is GET. Build the exclusion from the affected client's full URI set (Q-03 (QA-03 / QI-03)): every non-HTML path it hits must be covered, including `/` or page paths it calls with a non-HTML `Accept`, not just an API prefix; the `Accept` and method conditions cover those when the path list cannot. For a managed sub-rule with a Challenge action (for example Bot Control `TGT_*`), use R-01's shape: override the sub-rule to Count and apply Challenge in a custom rule after the group on its label with these conditions.
     96	
     97	**Effect:** eliminates the lockout for non-HTML and API requests. Those requests are then no longer challenged, so pair this with R-07 for API endpoints if they need protection.
     98	
     99	**Count-first validation:** for a custom Challenge or CAPTCHA rule, add the narrowed condition as a separate Count rule next to it and confirm it matches the browser page loads and none of the API or non-GET requests seen in Q-05 (QA-05 / QI-05), then replace the rule's condition. For a managed sub-rule, follow R-01's label-rule sequence (a challenge also ends evaluation, so a later label rule cannot see challenged requests until the sub-rule is in Count): override the sub-rule to Count and add the label rule in Count together, review, then switch the label rule to Challenge. The sub-rule challenges nobody in between, so keep that window short as described in R-01.
     100	
     101	---
     102	
     103	## R-06 - Client integration for token acquisition, and `TokenDomains`
     104	
     105	**When it applies:** the challenged clients are your own browser single-page application or mobile app, and they must keep passing Challenge or CAPTCHA (for example Bot Control targeted rules or Anti-DDoS soft mitigation).
     106	
     107	**Change (prose):** integrate the AWS WAF client application integration: the JavaScript integration for browser apps (it acquires the token and attaches it to fetch calls), or the AWS WAF mobile SDK for Android and iOS apps. For apps that span several subdomains or domains, set the Web ACL's `TokenDomains` to include every domain that should accept the token, so tokens acquired on one host are not `rejected:domain_mismatch` on another.
     108	
     109	**Effect:** eliminates `TOKEN_MISSING` and domain-mismatch failures for clients that integrate. It does not help third-party scripts or partners you cannot change (use R-05 or R-07 for them).
     110	
     111	**Count-first validation:** with the integration released, check in logs that the clients carry `awswaf:managed:token:accepted` (Q-09 (QA-09 / QI-09), Q-05 (QA-05 / QI-05)) while the rule is still in Count or scoped to a test path, before enforcing it widely.
     112	
     113	---
     114	
     115	## R-07 - Block or rate-based rule instead of Challenge on machine-to-machine endpoints
     116	
     117	**When it applies:** an endpoint is called by scripts, servers or partners that will never run a challenge, and the endpoint still needs protection.
     118	
     119	**Change (prose):** exclude the endpoint from Challenge and CAPTCHA (R-05), and protect it instead with rules that do not need client cooperation: a rate-based rule with action Block scoped to the endpoint, Block rules on labels from managed groups, or authentication at the API layer.
     120	
     121	**Effect:** eliminates the challenge lockout; reduces abuse risk on the endpoint to what the replacement rules catch.
     122	
     123	**Count-first validation:** run the rate-based rule in Count for a representative period and confirm the limit sits above legitimate peak rates per aggregation key (Q-11 (QA-11 / QI-11) for per-IP rates, Q-13 (QA-13 / QI-13) for top talkers).
     124	
     125	---
     126	
     127	## R-08 - Shield Advanced L7AM: action to Count, or migrate to the Anti-DDoS managed rule group
     128	
     129	**When it applies:** Shield Advanced automatic application layer DDoS mitigation blocks legitimate clients, for example blocks that continue after `DDoSDetected` returns to 0 on traffic that matches the pre-event baseline.
     130	
     131	**Change (prose):** these are the documented options. (a) In the Shield Advanced protection for the affected resource, change the automatic application layer mitigation action from Block to Count. Mitigation rules keep matching and can be watched in logs (Q-14b: QA-14b / QI-14b) but no longer block. (b) Migrate from L7AM to the AWS WAF Anti-DDoS managed rule group (`AWSManagedRulesAntiDDoSRuleSet`). The AWS WAF Developer Guide states that from March 26, 2026 the Anti-DDoS managed rule group became the default solution for HTTP request flood protection and supersedes L7AM; existing Shield Advanced customers can keep using L7AM (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/ddos-automatic-app-layer-response.html). The rule group offers soft (Challenge) and hard (Block) mitigation with tunable sensitivity (R-09). Do not edit the `ShieldMitigationRuleGroup_*` rule group itself; Shield manages it.
     132	
     133	**Effect:** (a) eliminates the false-positive blocks but also removes automatic blocking during future events, so state that trade-off. (b) reduces false positives through tunable sensitivity and exemptions while keeping automatic mitigation.
     134	
     135	**Count-first validation:** with (a), the Count mode itself is the validation: watch QA-14b / QI-14b during the next event to see what would have been blocked. With (b), add the Anti-DDoS rule group with its rules overridden to Count first and review its labels and matches before enforcing.
     136	
     137	---
     138	
     139	## R-09 - Anti-DDoS rule group tuning
     140	
     141	**When it applies:** the Anti-DDoS managed rule group challenges or blocks legitimate clients during events: intermittent lockouts on API paths, or broad challenges of all traffic.
     142	
     143	**Change (prose):**
     144	
     145	- **Exempt non-challengeable paths.** Add exempt URI regular expressions (`ExemptUriRegularExpressions` in the rule group's `ClientSideActionConfig`) for paths that cannot take a challenge (APIs, health checks, partner callbacks). Documented behavior (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/APIReference/API_ClientSideAction.html and https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/aws-managed-rule-groups-anti-ddos.html):
     146	  - The regex is matched against the request's host immediately followed by its normalized URI path, without scheme, query string or fragment (for example `www.example.com/api/orders`). A pattern anchored to the start of the path, such as `^/api/`, never matches.
     147	  - The path is normalized first (empty segments, including a trailing slash, and `.` segments removed, `..` resolved), so `/api/` is evaluated as `/api`.
     148	  - Only `GET` requests are challengeable; the `challengeable-request` label is never added to other methods.
     149	  - Requests that match an exempt regex are not evaluated by `ChallengeAllDuringEvent` or `ChallengeDDoSRequests`, whatever their action overrides. The documentation describes the exemption only for these two challenge rules, so do not assume it exempts requests from `DDoSRequests` (Block).
     150	  - The documented starting point is `\/api(\/|$)|\.(acc|avi|css|gif|jpe?g|js|mp[34]|ogg|otf|pdf|png|tiff?|ttf|webm|webp|woff2?)$`, to be reviewed for the application. Between 1 and 5 regexes are allowed.
     151	  - The `Accept` header is not part of the exempt match. Whether a challenged client can actually show the interstitial still depends on the general Challenge behavior (it is served only when `Accept` includes `text/html`).
     152	- **Use sensitivity-based challenges instead of challenging everything.** `ChallengeAllDuringEvent` challenges every challengeable request while the resource is under attack. Override it to Count so that `ChallengeDDoSRequests` is evaluated (it is evaluated only when the previous rule is overridden to Count), and tune the challenge `Sensitivity` in `ClientSideActionConfig` (LOW matches only high-suspicion requests, MEDIUM matches medium and high, HIGH, the default, matches all suspicion levels) so that only suspected attack sources are challenged. Tune `SensitivityToBlock`, used by `DDoSRequests`, the same way if blocks hit baseline clients.
     153	
     154	**Effect:** exemptions eliminate challenge lockouts on the exempted paths (they lose soft mitigation); sensitivity tuning reduces collateral challenges during events.
     155	
     156	**Count-first validation:** review the rule group's labels (`event-detected`, `ddos-request` with low, medium or high suspicion, `challengeable-request`) in logs (Q-09 (QA-09 / QI-09), Q-10 (QA-10 / QI-10)) to see which clients each sensitivity level would hit before changing it. Confirm that the exempt pattern removes `challengeable-request` from the intended paths only.
     157	
     158	---
     159	
     160	## R-10 - Rate-based rule in Count that matches abuse: switch to a scoped Block
     161	
     162	**When it applies:** a rate-based rule in Count matches abusive traffic (detected but not stopped), for example card testing on a payment endpoint or credential stuffing on login, seen in Q-08 (QA-08 / QI-08) and `ratebasedrulelist`. A client whose Q-08c burst is concentrated on a payment, checkout, login, signup or password-reset URI qualifies whatever its size; the fix for it is this pattern scoped to that URI (a new path-scoped rate-based rule, validated in Count first, if the existing rule is site-wide). Excluding a known-automation IP from the site-wide rule may be needed before any Block, but it is not the fix for the abuse.
     163	
     164	**Change (prose):** switch the rate-based rule to Block, scoped with a scope-down statement to the abused path (for example the payment or login endpoint) rather than the whole site. Choose aggregation keys that separate abusers from legitimate users behind shared egress: client IP when sources are distinct, the forwarded IP header when a trusted proxy or CDN sits in front, or custom keys (for example a session cookie, an API key header, or IP combined with a header) when many users share one NAT or corporate address. Set the limit from observed legitimate peak rates, not from the abuser's rate.
     165	
     166	**Effect:** reduces the abuse to the rate limit on that path; it does not eliminate low-and-slow abuse below the limit (check Q-11 (QA-11 / QI-11)).
     167	
     168	**Never** recommend switching a site-wide rate-based rule to Block when a known-automation client or a shared egress IP (NAT, corporate proxy) exceeds the limit: that blocks legitimate traffic. Scope it to the abused path, or exclude the verified automation with a scope-down, first. Say so explicitly in the output, naming the client: "Switching the site-wide rate-based rule <rule> from Count to Block is not recommended: it would block <client> (<known automation or shared egress>), which exceeds the limit." List the path-scoped rule for a card-testing or credential-stuffing burst first among the mitigations.
     169	
     170	**Count-first validation:** the rule is already in Count; before switching, confirm which keys exceeded the limit and that none of them are known legitimate automation (Q-13 (QA-13 / QI-13) with corroboration) or shared egress used by many real users (Q-08c (QA-08c / QI-08c) lists the keys per client).
     171	
     172	---
     173	
     174	## R-11 - WAF-layer and application-layer mitigations for abuse
     175	
     176	**When it applies:** traffic is judged `CORRECT_MITIGATION` but part of it gets through (detected-not-blocked, Count rules, valid tokens, attacker residue, card testing or credential stuffing), or abuse rides on genuine tokens or on SDK and mobile clients that WAF cannot challenge. Present recommendations under a "Recommended mitigations" heading with two sub-headings, "WAF layer" and "Application layer", and mark each as reduces or eliminates for the observed pattern.
     177	
     178	**WAF layer**
     179	
     180	- Close enforcement gaps: reference firing labels in a Block rule, or change offending rule actions from Count or CAPTCHA to Block, scoped narrowly (geography + endpoint + label) to limit collateral impact.
     181	- Endpoint and geography-scoped rule: geography AND URI AND an OR of the relevant labels.
     182	- Rate-based rules with appropriate aggregation keys (IP, forwarded IP, or custom keys) for volumetric patterns (see R-10).
     183	- **Attacker residue** (Q-19 (QA-19 / QI-19)): the allowed requests carry no labels, so a rule that matches labels cannot catch them. Match the request component the residue used: for a query-argument residue, a string or regex match statement on query arguments scoped to the affected path, or the managed sub-rule that inspects the query string (for example `LFI_QUERYSTRING` in `AWSManagedRulesLinuxRuleSet`); for a URI-path residue, the matching `_URIPATH` sub-rule or a scoped URI-path match. A `UriPath` rule never covers a query-argument residue.
